protections: P1: names of headers/parameters arriving from an untrusted transport must be rejected on the in-direction (applyFilterToExternalHeaders) whenever they carry the Camel prefix set, so they never become Camel message headers that a later endpoint (e.g. an HTTP/CoAP producer) reads back.

P2: the Camel-prefix test must be genuinely case-insensitive, not an enumeration of spellings ('Camel', 'camel', 'org.apache.camel.'), because Camel messages store headers in a case-insensitive map (DefaultMessage -> CaseInsensitiveMap), so any casing of an injected name is retrievable under the canonical Camel header key.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The Uri-Query to Camel-header mapping is the component's only way to hand request parameters to a route (the shipping REST test depends on ?id=Ducky arriving as header 'id'), CoAP is not one of the HTTP transports named by CVE-2025-27636, and neither CoAPEndpoint nor CoAPComponent implements HeaderFilterStrategyAware, so an audit that starts from the *HeaderFilterStrategy classes never visits this file.

The constant visibly lists both 'Camel' and 'camel' and its javadoc announces exactly those spellings, so the guard looks case-insensitive at a glance; only a reader who notices that tryHeaderMatch does a raw String.startsWith over three literals (and that the deprecated-pattern fast path repeats the same three literals) sees that 'CAMEL...', 'cAmel...' and 'ORG.APACHE.CAMEL.' are still copied into the case-insensitive message header map.

UndertowHeaderFilterStrategy does call setOutFilterStartsWith(CAMEL_FILTER_STARTS_WITH) and the binding does call applyFilterToExternalHeaders for request headers, query parameters and form data, so the component reads as protected; the guard is only the out-direction one, and Direction.IN reads inFilterStartsWith, which is never set, so even an exact-case 'CamelHttpPath' request header reaches the Camel message.

The CXF-RS binding already routes inbound protocol headers through applyFilterToExternalHeaders and its default strategy configures a Camel-prefix filter, so the call site looks protected; the configured filter is outFilterStartsWith only, so the check at DefaultCxfRsBinding:321 can never reject an inbound Camel header, and the whole thing lives in camel-cxf rather than in the HTTP transport family the report names.

This strategy implements the same Camel-prefix guard a second time as a case-insensitive (?i) regular expression, which looks stronger than the three-spelling startsWith list, so a solver who asks 'does it handle case?' answers yes; the regex is installed as outFilterPattern only, while the consumer's inbound loops over request headers and query parameters read the in direction, where nothing is configured.

Both are helper copies/removals that run only after the header filter strategy has already seen a header, so a solver can argue the strategy (T2) is the only place that decides; they nevertheless hard-code a third and fourth case-sensitive startsWith("Camel"), which a case-insensitive policy has to replace and which let a mixed-case Camel header ride along in the netty proxy response message.

conflicts.what: The cheapest fix for T2 is one shared, case-insensitive Camel-prefix rule in DefaultHeaderFilterStrategy; if T1 is then fixed by giving the CoAP consumer an instance of that strategy and letting it see the whole message, the same rule also drops the camel-prefixed response headers the consumer must read to build the reply (CamelCoapMaxAge at CamelCoapResource:143, CamelCoapETag at :148, CamelContentType), because those names are intentionally Camel-internal (CoAPConstants:45,47,51,55). The T1 fix must filter only while copying the request's Uri-Query options, never the routed message.

fairness_risks: CoAP query parameters map to headers by design and the existing REST fixture sends ?id=Ducky and reads header 'id' (CoAPRestComponentTestBase:60,136-137); a rule that drops or renames all query parameters, rather than only Camel-prefixed names, breaks a supported use.

The CoAP response is driven by camel-prefixed headers set by the route (CamelCoapMaxAge, CamelCoapETag, CamelCoapMethod, CamelCoapResponseCode; CoAPConstants:45-57, read at CamelCoapResource:143-153); a security rule that strips camel-prefixed headers from the message (or applies the out-direction filter to the CoAP path) breaks documented response control and the existing test that echoes Content-Type (CoAPRestComponentTestBase:140-145).

A case-insensitive Camel-prefix rule refuses names such as 'camelCaseId' or 'CamelBackupPath' that an application may legitimately use as its own header/parameter data; the strategy has no allow-list or keep-mode on the in direction, so those values are silently lost.

Undertow/HTTP REST endpoints declare query parameters and rely on filterCheck to keep their template/query tokens (UndertowRestHeaderFilterStrategy:34-37, UndertowComponent:333); a blanket in-direction Camel-prefix filter silently drops a declared parameter whose name happens to begin with 'camel'.

Adding the missing in-direction filter to a shared strategy instance also changes the producer side of the same component (Undertow's binding and Knative's producer use one strategy object for both directions), so camel-prefixed CloudEvent/extension headers that a route expects to forward stop being forwarded.

design.why: T2 is the only route where a single correct edit (a genuinely case-insensitive prefix match in DefaultHeaderFilterStrategy:56,382-390, plus the duplicate fast path at :368-379) closes every casing variant at once, so a stack made only of casing variants collapses into one trap; T1, T3, T4 and T5 cannot be closed by that edit or by each other because the CoAP resource has no filter strategy at all and the Undertow, CXF-RS and Knative strategies never set an in-direction guard (they only configure the out direction), so each needs its own change in a different module with a different configuration idiom. The five traps carry four distinct reasons to dismiss (a documented feature on a non-HTTP protocol; 'the list already has Camel and camel'; 'the strategy sets the prefix filter and the binding calls applyFilterToExternalHeaders'; 'the regex is case-insensitive') and two mechanisms (M8 shared-check shape, M4 absent route, M1 parallel transport, M2 second implementation), giving both a deepseek-style absent-route judgement and a mimo-style over-hardening hazard (T1's coupled CamelCoap* response headers, recorded as the T1/T2 conflict). A design of only T2+T6 (both case-sensitive prefix checks) is weaker: both are case variants of one idea and T6 has no reachable security effect once T2 is fixed.
